8. 
The Continued Vitality of the State Farm Approach. The relatively 
aggressive and minute manner in which the State Farm majority enforced the 
arbitrary-or-capricious standard continues to gamer support in today’s 
Supreme Court. The latest example is Ohio v. ERA, 144 S.Ct. 2040 (2024). As 
authorized by the Clean Air Act, EPA set a standard for the pollutant ozone, 
which triggered an obhgation for state governments to submit state 
implementation plans (SIPs) to meet the standard. The Act contains a Good 
Neighbor Provision that requires each state in its SIP to limit emissions so as 
not to interfere with the effort of downwind states to meet the standard. 
Several states submitted SIPs that EPA rejected on the ground that they failed 
to meet the obligations of the Good Neighbor Provision. EPA also proposed, for 
pubhc comment, a Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) to govern the 23 states 
that, in EPA’s view, did not have sufficient SIPs in place. While this 
rulemaking to estabhsh the FIP was proceeding, some states brought court 
challenges to EPA s rejections of their respective SIPs and got the rejections 
stayed. This raised the possibihty that the FIP would end up applying to fewer 
than the 23 states to which it initially seemed it would apply. When EPA 
promulgated the FIP as a final rule, several states went to the D.C. Circuit to 
challenge the FIP as arbitrary and capricious. The states asked for a stay of 
the FIP, which the D.C. Circuit refused. The states then apphed to the 
Supreme Court for a stay, which granted it pending the D.C. Circuit’s 
disposition of the case.
In granting the stay, the Supreme Court majority indicated that the 
states likelihood of success on the merits was the decisive factor. The majority 
said the states were likely to succeed on their arbitrary-or-capricious cb a Henge 
because (1) the FIP when formulated was premised on the assumption that it 
would cover 23 states and (2) the agency failed to respond to the states’ 
comment that the methodology behind the FIP would be vitiated if fewer than 
23 states ended up being covered, as was quite possible. As Justice Gorsuch 
wrote for the majority:
